name: authunix_refresh
prose: Refresh callback of the AUTH_UNIX client handle (auth_unix.c:245-284) for a rejected credential. If auth->ah_cred.oa_base already equals au->au_origcred.oa_base (the original credential is in use) it returns FALSE immediately without changing anything. Otherwise it increments au->au_shfaults (there is no limit check on it), decodes the original credential bytes with xdr_authunix_parms into a local struct, and if that fails goes to done. On success it sets aup_time to the current time, rewinds the XDR stream to the start, re-encodes the parameters in place over the original credential buffer, and if that fails goes to done; on success it sets auth->ah_cred to au->au_origcred and calls marshal_new_auth to rebuild the marshalled form. At done it frees the decoded parameters with an XDR_FREE pass, destroys the stream and returns the last xdr status: TRUE after a complete refresh, FALSE if either xdr_authunix_parms call failed (in the second-call failure case the original credential buffer may already have been partly overwritten, and ah_cred is left unchanged).
note: auth_unix.c:245-284 read in full. Reviewers wrong: there is no check of au_shfaults against MAX_AUTH_BYTES in this function (the counter is only incremented at 257, and MAX_AUTH_BYTES appears only in marshal_new_auth), and the already-original case returns FALSE, not TRUE (253-255).

name: clntraw_call
prose: RPC call routine of the "raw" in-process client (clnt_raw.c:133-222) that sends a call through the in-memory buffer to a server running in the same process. It reads the module-global clntraw_private into clp and computes &clp->xdr_stream before testing clp (a pointer computation, not a read); if clp is NULL it returns RPC_FAILED. At call_again it sets the XDR stream to encode and position 0, increments the message xid, and writes the pre-built call header bytes, the procedure number, the auth marshalled credentials (AUTH_MARSHALL) and the arguments (xargs); if any step fails it returns RPC_CANTENCODEARGS. It then runs the server side with svc_getreq(1), sets the stream to decode at position 0, and decodes the reply message with xdr_replymsg into msg with the result pointers; if that fails it frees what was decoded (an XDR_FREE pass) and returns RPC_CANTDECODERES. Otherwise it translates the reply with gssrpc__seterr_reply and takes the status from it. If the status is RPC_SUCCESS it validates the reply verifier with AUTH_VALIDATE (a failure makes the status RPC_AUTHERROR); for any other status it calls AUTH_REFRESH and, if that returns true, jumps back to call_again (retrying with a new xid). For a status still RPC_SUCCESS the validation is run a second time (lines 211-214) and the reply verifier is freed with xdr_opaque_auth. It returns the resulting status, which can be RPC_SUCCESS, a server-reported error status from the reply, or RPC_AUTHERROR.
note: clnt_raw.c:133-222 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (error statuses come through gssrpc__seterr_reply, 198-199); reviewer 2 only partly right: xdrs is computed from clp before the NULL test (143-144) but the test at 150 then returns RPC_FAILED, no dereference happens before it.

name: clnt_broadcast
prose: Broadcasts a portmapper CALLIT request for (prog, vers, proc) and passes each reply to a callback (pmap_rmt.c:228-416; the slice cut the head). It creates a default AUTH_UNIX handle, creates a UDP socket (failure: perror and RPC_CANTSEND) and enables SO_BROADCAST (failure: RPC_CANTSEND), collects the broadcast network addresses with getbroadcastnets, builds a call message with an xid derived from the pid and time and encodes the call header and the remote-call arguments into outbuf (failure: RPC_CANTENCODEARGS). It then makes rounds with select timeouts of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. In each round it sends the packet to every broadcast address with sendto (a send that does not return exactly the packet length gives RPC_CANTSEND); if eachresult is NULL it then returns RPC_SUCCESS right after the first round's sends. Otherwise it waits with select: a timeout sets the status to RPC_TIMEDOUT and starts the next round; EINTR retries the select; another select error gives RPC_CANTRECV. When the socket is readable it calls recvfrom (EINTR retried; another error gives RPC_CANTRECV); a datagram shorter than 4 bytes is ignored and the wait continues; for a longer one it decodes the reply and, if the xid matches, the reply is MSG_ACCEPTED and the accept status is SUCCESS, it sets the port in the reply address and calls eachresult(resultsp, &raddr), taking its non-zero return as done. For every datagram of at least 4 bytes it then frees the decoded reply with an XDR_FREE pass and invokes xresults with the XDR_FREE stream on resultsp. If done is set it returns RPC_SUCCESS; otherwise it waits for more replies in the same round. When all six rounds time out the loop ends and the last status, RPC_TIMEDOUT, is returned. On every return after the call handle was created, done_broad closes the socket (including after a failed socket() call) and destroys the AUTH handle with AUTH_DESTROY, which is not guarded against a NULL handle returned by authunix_create_default.
note: pmap_rmt.c:228-416 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer right (a datagram shorter than 4 bytes at 377-378 jumps back to recv_again before xresults at 403 is called).

name: svc_do_xprt
prose: Static function in svc.c (lines 447-536) that serves the requests ready on one transport. It allocates three buffers (raw credential and raw verifier of MAX_AUTH_BYTES each and a cooked credential area of RQCRED_SIZE); if any allocation fails it returns at once, leaking the ones that succeeded and leaving the transport untouched. It then loops: it calls SVC_RECV(xprt, &msg) and, if that fails, goes to call_done without dispatching; otherwise it fills a struct svc_req from the message and calls gssrpc__authenticate. If authentication fails it sends svcerr_auth with the reason and goes to call_done; if it succeeds but sets no_dispatch it goes to call_done without replying here. Otherwise it searches the registered callouts for the program and version: an exact match calls its dispatch function and goes to call_done; if the program exists with other versions it sends svcerr_progvers with the lowest and highest registered versions, and if the program is unknown it sends svcerr_noprog. At call_done it reads SVC_STAT(xprt): if the transport has died (XPRT_DIED) it calls SVC_DESTROY(xprt) and leaves the loop; otherwise, if xprt->xp_auth is non-NULL and its ops are not the GSS ops, it sets xp_auth to NULL. The loop repeats while the status is XPRT_MOREREQS. After the loop (not on the early allocation-failure return) it frees the three buffers.
note: svc.c:446-536 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (an allocation failure returns without freeing the buffers that were allocated, 462-463, and the no_dispatch case sends no reply, 491-492); reviewer 2 wrong: SVC_DESTROY(xprt) is called when the status is XPRT_DIED (524-526).

name: gssrpc__svcauth_gss
prose: Server-side RPCSEC_GSS authentication for one received call (svc_auth_gss.c:387-555), returning an auth_stat and possibly setting *no_dispatch. It first resets the transport verifier xp_verf to the null auth. If the transport has no auth or svc_auth_none it callocs an auth and a data structure and installs them in xp_auth (an allocation failure returns AUTH_FAILED, and a failure of the second calloc leaks the first block); otherwise it uses the existing data. An empty credential gives AUTH_BADCRED; the credential is decoded into the svc_req's cooked credential area (a decode failure gives AUTH_BADCRED). The remaining checks free the decoded credential on exit. A wrong gc_v version or an invalid gc_svc service gives AUTH_BADCRED. For an established context: a sequence number above MAXSEQ gives RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM; the replay window is updated (a newer number shifts the window), and a number outside the window or already seen sets *no_dispatch to 1 and gives RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM; otherwise the sequence is recorded; the client name and context are copied into the request. Then by gc_proc: for RPCSEC_GSS_INIT and RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT a call procedure other than NULLPROC, a failed credential acquire or a failed verifier generation gives AUTH_FAILED, a failed context accept gives AUTH_REJECTEDCRED; otherwise it sets *no_dispatch, sends the init reply (a failed send gives AUTH_FAILED), releases the buffers, and marks the context established when the major status is GSS_S_COMPLETE. For RPCSEC_GSS_DATA it validates the request MIC (failure gives RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM) and builds the next verifier (failure AUTH_FAILED). For RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY it requires NULLPROC (else AUTH_FAILED), validates the MIC (RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM on failure), builds the verifier (AUTH_FAILED), sets *no_dispatch, sends an empty reply (its result is not checked), destroys the auth handle and sets xp_auth to &svc_auth_none. Any other procedure gives AUTH_REJECTEDCRED. The successful cases return AUTH_OK.
note: svc_auth_gss.c:387-555 read in full, with debug logging lines skipped. Reviewer 1 right (RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM for bad or replayed sequence numbers, 460-471); reviewer 2 mixed: a failed MIC validation returns RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM (517-518, 528-529), not AUTH_BADCRED, and an unknown procedure returns AUTH_REJECTEDCRED (546-547), not AUTH_FAILED.

name: gssrpc__svcauth_gssapi
prose: Server-side AUTH_GSSAPI (the older GSS RPC flavor) authentication of one call (svc_auth_gssapi.c:156-660; the real name is gssrpc__svcauth_gssapi). It cleans up expired client records, sets xp_auth to &svc_auth_none and decodes the credential from the message. An empty credential gives AUTH_BADCRED, an undecodable one AUTH_BADCRED (after freeing it), and a version other than 2 gives AUTH_BADCRED. For an AUTH_GSSAPI_INIT call with auth_msg set it requires an empty client handle (else AUTH_FAILED) and creates a client record (AUTH_FAILED on failure); otherwise it requires a non-empty handle (AUTH_FAILED) and looks the client up (AUTH_BADCRED if unknown). It then sets xp_auth to the client's svcauth. If the context is not yet established it returns AUTH_REJECTEDCRED when auth_msg is false, AUTH_FAILED unless the procedure is AUTH_GSSAPI_INIT or AUTH_GSSAPI_CONTINUE_INIT, and AUTH_BADCRED when the init arguments cannot be decoded; an unsupported init version gives AUTH_BADCRED (versions 1 and 2 are accepted with a warning, 3 and 4 are used as is) and, for version 3 and later, a missing local address gives AUTH_FAILED; these two failure returns do not free the decoded init arguments (only the credential is freed at the error label). It then runs gss_accept_sec_context, trying the client's server credentials or each configured credential in turn, and frees the init arguments. If the accept fails (major status neither COMPLETE nor CONTINUE_NEEDED) it calls badauth, releases the output token, sends the init reply, sets *no_dispatch to TRUE and returns AUTH_OK (the error label then returns ret, which is AUTH_OK). Otherwise it stores the output token, on completion seals the initial sequence number (failure: release the token, AUTH_FAILED), sends the reply, sets *no_dispatch, and marks the client established when the status is GSS_S_COMPLETE. For an established context it unseals the verifier sequence number (failure: AUTH_BADVERF), requires it to equal the stored number plus one (else AUTH_REJECTEDVERF, calling log_badverf), releases the previous verifier and seals the response sequence number (failure: AUTH_FAILED); for an auth_msg call it then handles AUTH_GSSAPI_MSG (decode arguments, BADCRED on failure, process the token, AUTH_FAILED unless the status is GSS_S_COMPLETE, reply and set *no_dispatch) and AUTH_GSSAPI_DESTROY (reply and set *no_dispatch, then clean up the client), and any other procedure gives AUTH_FAILED. Success returns AUTH_OK; the credential is freed on the exit paths.
note: Partly read: svc_auth_gssapi.c:156-340 in full and a goto/ret/call skeleton of 340-660 (the credential search loop at 345-450 and the message processing at 560-640 not read line by line). Reviewer 1 right (the accept-failure path sends a reply, sets *no_dispatch and returns AUTH_OK, 453-466); reviewer 2 right (the bad-version and missing-address returns at 337-341 and 361-364 do not free the decoded call_arg). The old prose also named AUTH_BADCRED and AUTH_REJECTEDCRED for the established-context verifier failures, which actually return AUTH_BADVERF (521) and AUTH_REJECTEDVERF (534).

name: krb5_decode_princ_entry
prose: Decodes a stored V1 principal record content into a new krb5_db_entry (kdb_xdr.c:225-442; the real name is krb5_decode_princ_entry). It sets *entry_ptr to NULL, allocates the entry (the allocation error is returned) and walks the content bytes while tracking sizeleft. A record shorter than KRB5_KDB_V1_BASE_LENGTH gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD. It reads the length, attributes, lifetimes, expiration times, last success and failure times, failure count and the tl_data and key_data counts; a negative n_tl_data or n_key_data gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD. If the stored length exceeds the base length it copies the extra bytes as e_data (length len - base length) with k5memdup, without checking them against sizeleft (an allocation failure returns that error). It then requires at least 2 bytes for the name length and a NUL-terminated name of that length with no embedded NUL inside the declared size (else KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD) and parses it with krb5_parse_name (its error is returned). It reads each tl_data node (4 bytes header; a short header or a length beyond sizeleft gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD, a failed malloc gives ENOMEM, contents copied with k5memdup) and allocates the key_data array (ENOMEM) and reads each key: a short 4-byte header gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD, a key_data_ver outside 0..KRB5_KDB_V1_KEY_DATA_ARRAY gives KRB5_KDB_BAD_VERSION, and for each of the ver parts it reads type and length (truncation checks against sizeleft) and copies non-empty contents with k5memdup. On success it stores the entry in *entry_ptr and returns 0; on any error it frees the partly built entry with krb5_db_free_principal, leaves *entry_ptr NULL and returns the error code.
note: kdb_xdr.c:225-442 read in full, comments skipped. Fixed under the real name; the only recorded reviewer reason was the mechanical name rejection. Note added vs. the old prose: the e_data copy at 314-320 is not bounds-checked against the remaining content size.

name: kdb5_ldap_create_policy
prose: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util create_policy command (kdb5_ldap_policy.c:92-310, void return); argv[1..] hold the options and the policy DN. A usage error occurs when argc is outside 2..16, when -maxtktlife or -maxrenewlife has no following value, when a ticket-flag option name is matched but its first character is neither '+' nor '-', when the DN is given twice (any argument that is not a known option is taken as the policy DN) and when no DN was given. A usage error sets print_usage (and suppresses the generic message) and leads to cleanup, where db_usage(CREATE_POLICY) is called, with retval 0 so exit_status is not incremented. It callocs the policy parameters (ENOMEM: goes to cleanup with the generic message "while creating policy object" and exit_status++). It parses -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife with get_date (an unparsable value sets EINVAL, prints "while providing time specification" and increments exit_status), computes the lifetime as the date minus now, and sets or clears the ticket-flag bits for the +/- options (allow_postdated, allow_forwardable, allow_renewable, allow_proxiable, allow_dup_skey, requires_preauth, requires_hwauth, allow_svr, allow_tgs_req, allow_tix, needchange, password_changing_service), recording the fields in the mask. For the DN it duplicates the argument (strdup failure: ENOMEM message "while creating policy object", exit_status++). It then calls init_ldap_realm (failure: message "while reading realm information", exit_status++) and krb5_ldap_create_policy (failure: its error is printed once with "while creating policy object" and exit_status++). cleanup frees the parameters with krb5_ldap_free_policy, prints usage if requested, and increments exit_status whenever retval is non-zero. On success it returns with exit_status unchanged.
note: kdb5_ldap_policy.c:92-310 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer wrong: an option such as "allow_postdated" with a first character other than '+' or '-' is matched by strcmp(argv[i] + 1, ...) (150) and then goes to err_usage (155-156); it is not taken as the policy DN. Fixed under the real name; the packet's name rejection was mechanical.

name: kdb5_ldap_modify_policy
prose: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util modify_policy command (kdb5_ldap_policy.c:420-669, void return; the real name is kdb5_ldap_modify_policy). If argc is outside 3..16 it goes to the usage path. Pass 1 scans all arguments only to find the policy DN: -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife skip their following argument, the known ticket-flag option names (matched on argv[i] + 1) are ignored, and any other argument is the DN; a second DN gives a usage error, a strdup failure gives ENOMEM with the message "while modifying policy object" and exit_status++, and no DN gives a usage error. It then calls init_ldap_realm (failure goes to cleanup, which prints "while modifying policy object" and increments exit_status) and reads the existing policy with krb5_ldap_read_policy (failure: message "while reading information of policy '<DN>'", exit_status++). Pass 2 re-scans the arguments, skipping the DN: -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife without a following value are usage errors, an unparsable date prints "while providing time specification" with exit_status++, otherwise the new lifetime is the date minus now; each ticket-flag option sets or clears the matching bit in the policy flags, with a first character other than '+' or '-' being a usage error; the changed fields are recorded in out_mask. It then calls krb5_ldap_modify_policy with out_mask (failure: cleanup prints "while modifying policy object" and increments exit_status). The usage path prints the modify_policy usage via db_usage without incrementing exit_status. cleanup always frees the policy parameters and the duplicated DN. On success it modifies on the server only the attributes recorded in out_mask and leaves exit_status unchanged.
note: kdb5_ldap_policy.c:420-669 read in full (the per-flag bit assignments were checked by their structure only). Reviewer wrong: a second DN is rejected in pass 1 at 466-467 with err_usage, and the pass-2 else at 633-636 only skips the (already accepted) DN, so it is not silently ignored.

name: kdb5_ldap_create
prose: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util create command (kdb5_ldap_realm.c:357-664, void return; the real name is kdb5_ldap_create). It callocs realm parameters (ENOMEM goes to cleanup) and parses the options: -subtrees, -containerref, -sscope, -s (stash), and ticket-policy options through get_ticket_policy, recording the chosen fields in mask; a missing option value or an unknown argument is a usage error. Unless a master password was already set it reads it with krb5_read_password (failure: message path). It then takes the LDAP context from the DAL handle (a NULL context goes to cleanup), reads the Kerberos container DN with krb5_ldap_read_krbcontainer_dn (or takes it from a given location), creates the container (krb5_ldap_create_krbcontainer) and the realm object (krb5_ldap_create_realm); after the realm object exists it sets realm_obj_created. It re-reads the realm parameters (a failure prints "while reading information of realm" and sets no_msg), replaces realm_name with a strdup of global_params.realm (ENOMEM on failure), builds the master key principal with krb5_db_setup_mkey_name, derives the master key from the password (salt with krb5_principal2salt, then krb5_c_string_to_key; each failure prints a message and sets no_msg), temporarily clears the realm's containerref and calls create_special_princs (restoring containerref afterwards; a failure prints "while adding entries to the database"), and then sets create_complete. If -s was given or KADM5_CONFIG_STASH_FILE is in the global mask it stores the master key with krb5_db_store_master_key using the user-specified kvno or 1; on failure it prints "while storing key" and a warning, but retval keeps the failing code. At cleanup it deletes the realm object with krb5_ldap_delete_realm when realm_obj_created is set and create_complete is not, frees the realm parameters, zeroes pw_str, prints usage if requested, and when retval is non-zero prints "while creating realm '<name>'" unless no_msg is set and increments exit_status. Afterwards it frees the master key contents and the master principal. Therefore a failed stash, which happens after create_complete, does not delete the realm but still prints the generic message and increments exit_status.
note: Partly read: kdb5_ldap_realm.c:357-400 and 520-664 in full, comments skipped; the option parsing and password section 400-520 only through a grep of its goto and mask lines. Reviewer right: the stash failure assigns the error to retval at 621 (it is not reset), so the cleanup block at 654-660 prints the generic message and increments exit_status; the old statement that exit_status is not incremented was wrong.

name: main
prose: Entry point of kdb5_ldap_util (kdb5_ldap_util.c:235-608) returning the global exit_status. It sets progname, initialises the Kerberos context (failure: message, exit_status++, cleanup) and allocates the sub-command argument array (ENOMEM: message, exit_status++). It parses the global options: -P (master password), -r (realm, also set as default realm), -k (enctype; an invalid one gives EINVAL, exit_status++ and cleanup), -kv (key version; the IGNORE_VNO value gives EINVAL and exit_status++), -M, -sf, -m, -D (bind DN), -w (password, strdup'ed), -H (server), --help (sets a flag), the first recognised sub-command name, and collects all other arguments as sub-command arguments; a second sub-command name, no sub-command, or --help frees the argument array and calls usage() and goes to cleanup without incrementing exit_status, so these paths can return 0. For sub-commands other than list and stashsrvpw it requires a default realm (failure: message and exit_status++). It reads the LDAP configuration section name from the profile, retrieves the config parameters (failure: message, exit_status++), initialises the LDAP library, allocates the LDAP context and fills in the bind password (prompting with krb5_read_password when only -D was given; a failed or empty read is reported with ENOMEM), the server list entry and the bind DN (each allocation failure: message, exit_status++). If the configured enctype is not valid it only prints a com_err message and continues. It then sets up the DAL library handle, installs the LDAP context in it, reads the server parameters (failure: message, exit_status++), opens the database when the sub-command needs it (failure: message, exit_status++), and runs the sub-command function with its arguments; the sub-command itself reports its failures by incrementing exit_status. Cleanup zeroes and frees the password, frees an unused LDAP context, frees the config params (unless static), finishes and frees util_context, frees the argument array, prompt and section name, and returns exit_status. usage_print is never set to a non-zero value in this function.
note: kdb5_ldap_util.c:235-608 read in full, comments skipped (the ARG_VAL macro and usage() body were not read, but usage does not touch exit_status per a grep of 100-235). Reviewer right: the --help and usage paths do not increment exit_status (356-357, 365-369, 375-379), so main can return 0 after printing usage.

name: populate_krb5_db_entry
prose: Fills a krb5_db_entry from an LDAP entry (ldap_misc.c:1410-1702; the real name is populate_krb5_db_entry, called with context, ldap_context, ld, the LDAP message ent, the principal princ and the output entry; no arguments are handed over to it). It copies princ into entry->princ, and when the LDAP entry has krbprincipalname values it unparses princ, counts the values if one matches, reads the entry DN (failure: LDAP error mapped and returned), records a standalone-object type tl_data if the objectclass list contains krbprincipal, and stores the principal count and DN in a local tl_data list. It then reads, each with its attribute-presence bit recorded in a local mask, krbLastSuccessfulAuth, krbLastFailedAuth, krbLoginFailedCount, krbmaxticketlife, krbmaxrenewableage, krbticketflags, krbprincipalexpiration and krbpasswordexpiration into the entry; the krbticketpolicyreference and krbpwdpolicyreference names (converted from DNs, failures returned); the password history (krb5_decode_histkey) and the kadm5 policy data (krb5_update_tl_kadm_data); the secret keys (krb5_decode_krbsecretkey, and the master key version with krb5_dbe_update_mkvno when non-zero); the last password change and last admin unlock times; the constrained-delegation values as KRB5_TL_CONSTRAINED_DELEGATION_ACL tl_data appended to entry->tl_data; the link references and krbExtraData items as tl_data; and the authentication indicators with get_ldap_auth_ind. It stores the mask as a KDB_TL_MASK tl_data and updates the entry's tl_data. A nsAccountLock attribute equal to "TRUE" (case-insensitive) sets KRB5_KDB_DISALLOW_ALL_TIX in entry->attributes. It then reads the ticket policy with krb5_read_tkt_policy and finally sets entry->len to KRB5_KDB_V1_BASE_LENGTH. Any failing step goes to cleanup with its error code (ENOMEM or the callee's code), leaving the entry partly filled in. Cleanup frees the DN, the LDAP value lists, the temporary tl_data contents, the policy names and strings, the unparsed name and the temporary policy record, and returns the code, 0 on success. The password history pointer ber_key_data is freed at line 1559 without being cleared, so a failure of krb5_update_tl_kadm_data before ber_key_data is assigned again would free it again at cleanup.
note: ldap_misc.c:1410-1702 read in full, comments skipped. Fixed under the real name; the packet's only reviewer reason was the mechanical name rejection. The old prose described a different signature (an owning transfer of dn, pnvalues, ocvalues, user and tktpolname), which is not the code in this tree.

name: verify_securid_data_2
prose: KDC-side verification of a SecurID SAM-2 preauth response (securid2.c:274-666; only built with ARL_SECURID_PREAUTH). It sets *sc2_out to NULL, unparses the client name (failure: message and immediate return of that error), and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED for an empty response ciphertext. It finds and decrypts the client key, decrypts the response (k5alloc, krb5_c_decrypt, decode failures returned) and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED for a nonce mismatch, an empty SAD or a SAD longer than the passcode buffer; it copies the SAD to passcode and the user name without the realm into securid_user (ENOMEM on strdup failure). If the response carries a track id it decrypts it (errors returned), requires the track data to be at least the structure size (KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), returns KRB5KDC_ERR_DISCARD when its host id differs from gethostid(), and switches on its state: SECURID_STATE_INITIAL jumps to the initial check; NEW_PIN_AGAIN compares the repeated PIN with the stored one (mismatch: KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), calls SD_Pin and SD_Close and on ACM_NEW_PIN_ACCEPTED sets TKT_FLG_HW_AUTH and TKT_FLG_PRE_AUTH in enc_tkt_reply and returns 0, else KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED; NEW_PIN builds a "new PIN again" challenge (random nonce failure, track-data encryption failure and sam_make_challenge failure are returned), stores it in *sc2_out and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; NEXT_CODE calls SD_Next and SD_Close and sets the two flags and returns 0 on ACM_OK, else KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED. A track state not listed here leaves the earlier result, 0, and returns it without setting the flags. Without track data it initialises the SecurID handle (SD_Init failure, then SD_Lock failure: KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), calls SD_Check: ACM_OK closes the handle, sets the two flags and returns 0; ACM_ACCESS_DENIED closes the handle and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED; ACM_NEW_PIN_REQUIRED or ACM_NEXT_CODE_REQUIRED builds a challenge (the handle is kept in the encrypted track data and not closed; a random nonce or track-encryption failure is returned), and a failure of sam_make_challenge there is only logged: the code then still stores sc2p in *sc2_out and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; any other SD_Check result returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED. On every path after the name was unparsed, cleanup frees the client key contents, the scratch buffer, the decoded response, the user strings, the track data and any unused challenge.
note: securid2.c:274-666 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (k5alloc, random and encryption errors are returned, and the SD handle stays open on the challenge path); reviewer 2 right (the sam_make_challenge failure in the initial branch at 630-635 is only logged and the function still returns PREAUTH_REQUIRED at 644, although in the NEW_PIN state the same failure goes to cleanup at 498-504).

name: getopt_long
prose: Fallback getopt_long for systems without one (getopt_long.c:157-231), built on getopt_internal (72-130) which keeps a static scan pointer and the globals optind, optopt, optarg and opterr. getopt_internal returns -1 when there are no more options, when the word does not start with '-', when the word is a lone "-" (a '-' option letter not listed in the option string), BADCH ('?') for an unknown or ':' option letter (advancing optind when the word is finished, with a diagnostic when opterr is set and the option string does not start with ':'), BADARG (':') (with the diagnostic only when the option string does not start with ':', in the else-branch of its test) for a short option missing its argument, the option letter otherwise (setting optarg to NULL, to the attached text, or to the next word and advancing optind), and -2 for a word beginning with "--" (leaving optind unchanged). For any other value getopt_long returns it unchanged. For -2 it takes the text after "--" from nargv[optind] and increments optind; an empty text (a bare "--") returns -1. It splits off a '=' value if present and searches long_options for the first entry whose name starts with the given text (the user text is a prefix of the option name; strncmp over the user text's length), preferring an entry whose name has exactly that length, with no check for ambiguity. If nothing matches it prints an "illegal option" diagnostic (when opterr is set and *options is not ':') and returns BADCH. For a match with required_argument or optional_argument it sets optarg to the text after '=' if there was one, else to nargv[optind] and increments optind (this reads nargv[optind] even when optind is at nargc, which relies on the vector being NULL-terminated; an optional argument therefore consumes the next word even if it looks like an option); for no_argument entries optarg is left as it was. A required_argument whose optarg is NULL prints the "requires an argument" diagnostic (opterr set and *options not ':') and returns BADARG; *index is not stored on the BADCH and BADARG returns. Otherwise if the entry has a flag pointer it stores the entry's val through it and returns 0, else it returns val, and stores the match index through *index when index is non-NULL.
note: getopt_long.c:72-130 and 157-231 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (short-option return paths); reviewer 2 right (no *index on BADARG, 204-215); reviewer 3 right (the match test strncmp(current_argv, name, current_argv_len) makes the user text a prefix of the option name, 185-195); the old prose also said optional_argument without '=' leaves optarg NULL, which is wrong because line 202 takes the next word.

name: mkstemp
prose: Fallback mkstemp (mkstemp.c:67-73) that calls _gettemp(path, &fd) and returns fd when _gettemp returns non-zero and -1 otherwise. path is modified in place by _gettemp. On success fd is a descriptor opened O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_RDWR with mode 0600 on the generated name, which the caller must close. A template without trailing 'X' characters is not rewritten and is opened as given. On failure no descriptor is returned and path may have been changed (trailing X characters replaced, or truncated at the last '/' when the directory check failed).
note: mkstemp.c:65-73 read in full; see _gettemp for the details. Reviewer 1 right (a path made only of X characters makes the backward scan in _gettemp read before the start of the string, and exhaustion returns EEXIST); reviewer 2 right (with no trailing X the path is not modified, and a directory stat failure leaves the path truncated at the slash).

name: _gettemp
prose: Static helper of the fallback mkstemp (mkstemp.c:75-138). It takes the pid, scans to the end of path and then backwards over trailing 'X' characters, replacing each with a decimal digit of the pid (least significant digit last X first). A path made only of X characters makes this backward scan run before the start of the string, which is undefined behaviour; a path without trailing X is left unmodified by this step. It then scans backwards for the last '/' before the X block: if it finds one it temporarily terminates the path there and calls stat; a stat failure returns 0 with the path left truncated at the slash (the slash is not restored) and errno from stat, and a non-directory sets errno to ENOTDIR and returns 0, also leaving the path truncated; otherwise the slash is restored. In a loop it then tries the name: if doopen is non-NULL it opens with O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_RDWR|O_BINARY, mode 0600, storing the descriptor in *doopen, and returns 1 on success, or 0 for an open error other than EEXIST (a failed open leaves *doopen negative); if doopen is NULL it calls stat and returns 1 when stat fails with ENOENT and 0 when it fails with another error, and continues when the file exists. To get the next name it steps the suffix characters starting at the first replaced position: 'z' becomes 'a' with a carry, a digit becomes 'a', any other character is incremented; when the carry runs off the end of the string it returns 0 (with errno EEXIST left from the last open in the open case, and unchanged from before the call in the stat case, since a successful stat does not set errno).
note: mkstemp.c:75-138 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (exhaustion with doopen NULL returns 0 without setting errno, and an all-X path reads before the buffer); reviewer 2 right (with no trailing X the call can return 1 with a path that was not modified at all, so "modified with a generated suffix" does not always hold).

name: ecb_bitrev32
prose: Pure helper of libev's ecb.h portion in ev.c (lines 1045-1055) that returns x with its 32 bits in reverse order (bit i of the result is bit 31 - i of x). It swaps adjacent bits, then 2-bit pairs, nibbles, bytes and finally the two 16-bit halves, using the masks 0x55555555, 0x33333333, 0x0f0f0f0f and 0x00ff00ff and a final 16-bit rotation. It accepts any uint32_t value, reads and writes nothing but its argument and returns the result.
note: ev.c:1045-1055 read in full. No reviewer claim beyond the earlier unreviewed state.

name: ecb_popcount64
prose: Pure helper (ev.c:1059-1064) returning the number of set bits of a 64-bit value as an int. It computes it as ecb_popcount32 of the low 32 bits (the argument converted to uint32_t) plus ecb_popcount32 of the high 32 bits (x >> 32); ecb_popcount32 itself was not read. It accepts any uint64_t value and has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1059-1064 read; ecb_popcount32 not read, so the result's correctness depends on it.

name: ecb_rotl8
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1075) that rotates the 8-bit value x left by count bits: it returns (x >> (8 - count)) | (x << count), converted to uint8_t on return (x is promoted to int first). It gives the left rotation for count from 0 to 8 inclusive; for count greater than 8 the shift amount 8 - count is negative, which is undefined. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1075 read. Fixed from the unreviewed text with the exact valid range for the promoted-int shifts.

name: ecb_rotr8
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1076) that rotates the 8-bit value x right by count bits: it returns (x << (8 - count)) | (x >> count), converted to uint8_t on return (x is promoted to int first). It gives the right rotation for count from 0 to 8 inclusive; for count greater than 8 the left shift amount is negative, which is undefined. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1076 read.

name: ecb_rotl16
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1077) that rotates the 16-bit value x left by count bits: it returns (x >> (16 - count)) | (x << count), converted to uint16_t on return (x is promoted to int first, so shifting by 16 is defined when int is 32 bits wide). It gives the left rotation for count from 0 to 16 inclusive; for count greater than 16 the right shift amount is negative, which is undefined. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1077 read; the 0 and 16 cases rely on x being promoted to a wider int.

name: ecb_rotr16
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1078) that rotates the 16-bit value x right by count bits: it returns (x << (16 - count)) | (x >> count), converted to uint16_t on return (x is promoted to int first). It gives the right rotation for count from 0 to 16 inclusive; for count greater than 16 the left shift amount is negative, which is undefined. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_rotl32
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1079) that rotates the uint32_t x left by count bits: it returns (x >> (32 - count)) | (x << count). It gives the correct left rotation for count from 1 to 31; with count 0 the right shift is by 32 and with count 32 the left shift is by 32, both undefined for a 32-bit unsigned operand, and larger counts make a shift amount negative or too large. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1079 read.

name: ecb_rotr32
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1080) that rotates the uint32_t x right by count bits: it returns (x << (32 - count)) | (x >> count). It gives the correct right rotation for count from 1 to 31; counts 0 and 32 and larger make a shift by the full width or a negative amount, which is undefined. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_rotl64
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1081) that rotates the uint64_t x left by count bits: it returns (x >> (64 - count)) | (x << count). It gives the correct left rotation for count from 1 to 63; counts 0 and 64 and larger shift by the full width or by a negative amount, which is undefined. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_rotr64
prose: Inline helper (ev.c:1082) that rotates the uint64_t x right by count bits: it returns (x << (64 - count)) | (x >> count). It gives the correct right rotation for count from 1 to 63; counts 0 and 64 and larger shift by the full width or by a negative amount, which is undefined. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_bswap16
prose: Byte swap of a 16-bit value in ev.c (lines 1084-1118). With GCC or clang builtins it is a macro for __builtin_bswap16 (or for __builtin_bswap32(x) >> 16 on older compilers), with MSVC it is a macro around _byteswap_ushort, and otherwise (lines 1098-1103) it is an inline function ecb_bswap16(uint16_t x) that returns ecb_rotl16(x, 8). In every variant the result is x with its two bytes exchanged (high byte and low byte swapped); the macro forms evaluate their argument as a plain expression. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1084-1118 read. The three compile-time variants are described because the function form exists only in the fallback branch.

name: ecb_bswap32
prose: Byte swap of a 32-bit value in ev.c (lines 1084-1118). With GCC or clang it is a macro for __builtin_bswap32, with MSVC a macro around _byteswap_ulong, and otherwise (1105-1110) an inline function ecb_bswap32(uint32_t x) returning (((uint32_t)ecb_bswap16 (x)) << 16) | ecb_bswap16 (x >> 16). In each variant the result is x with its four bytes in reverse order. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_bswap64
prose: Byte swap of a 64-bit value in ev.c (lines 1084-1118). With GCC or clang it is a macro for __builtin_bswap64, with MSVC a macro around _byteswap_uint64, and otherwise (1112-1117) an inline function ecb_bswap64(uint64_t x) returning (((uint64_t)ecb_bswap32 (x)) << 32) | ecb_bswap32 (x >> 32). In each variant the result is x with its eight bytes in reverse order. It has no side effects.

name: ecb_big_endian
prose: Inline function (ev.c:1159-1160) returning an ecb_bool: true when ecb_byteorder_helper() equals 0x11223344. The helper returns that constant on targets recognised at compile time as big-endian (__BYTE_ORDER__ or a list of big-endian architecture macros), returns 0x44332211 on recognised little-endian targets, and otherwise builds a union of the bytes 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44 at run time and returns the 32-bit value read from it. So it is true exactly when the byte layout reads as 0x11223344, and false for little-endian and for a target that is neither. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1131-1160 read in full. Fixed from the unreviewed text: it relies on the helper, with a compile-time shortcut and a run-time union fallback.

name: ecb_little_endian
prose: Inline function (ev.c:1161-1162) returning an ecb_bool: true when ecb_byteorder_helper() equals 0x44332211, i.e. when a 32-bit value built from the bytes 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44 in memory order reads back as 0x44332211. The helper decides this at compile time on recognised little- and big-endian targets and otherwise by a run-time union read. It is false on big-endian targets and on any target that is neither. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1131-1162 read in full.

name: ecb_binary16_to_binary32
prose: Pure function (ev.c:1197-1227) that converts the IEEE-754 half-precision bit pattern in the low 16 bits of x to the single-precision bit pattern of the same value (higher bits of x are ignored). It takes the sign bit, the 5-bit exponent and the 10-bit mantissa; an exponent of 31 (infinity or NaN) becomes exponent 255 with the mantissa kept, an exponent of 0 with a zero mantissa (zero) becomes exponent 0, an exponent of 0 with a non-zero mantissa (subnormal) is normalised by shifting the mantissa (using ecb_ld32, not read) and adjusting the exponent, and a normal exponent is rebiased by adding 127 - 15. It returns sign | (exponent << 23) | (mantissa << 13). It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1197-1227 read; ecb_ld32 not read.

name: ecb_binary32_to_binary16
prose: Pure function (ev.c:1229-1291) that converts the single-precision bit pattern x to the nearest half-precision bit pattern (returned as uint16_t). It keeps the sign. If |x| is in 0x38800000..0x477fefff (normal half range) it rounds the mantissa to 10 bits with round-half-to-even (adding 0xfff plus the lowest kept bit), bumps the exponent if rounding carries, and returns sign | (exponent << 10) | mantissa. If |x| is above 0x477fefff and up to 0x7f800000 (infinity) it returns signed infinity (0x7c00). If |x| is below 0x38800000 it returns signed zero for an exact zero or for exponents too small (e < 14 - 24), and otherwise forms a half subnormal by shifting the mantissa with the implicit bit and round-half-to-even. For |x| above 0x7f800000 (NaN) it returns sign | 0x7c00 | (mantissa >> 13), forced non-zero so the result stays a NaN. It has no side effects.
note: ev.c:1229-1291 read; the checks in the code are on the absolute value (x with the sign bit cleared at line 1237).

name: periodic_recalc
prose: Static function in libev (ev.c:3366-3388, only when EV_PERIODIC_ENABLE) that recomputes the next trigger time of periodic watcher w and stores it in ev_at(w); it returns nothing and uses the global current time ev_rt_now. It first computes interval as w->interval if that exceeds MIN_INTERVAL and MIN_INTERVAL otherwise, and a starting time at = offset + interval * floor((ev_rt_now - offset) / interval) (the comment says this usually errs on the low side). While at is less than or equal to ev_rt_now it computes nat = at + w->interval (the original interval, not the clamped one); if nat equals at (the addition no longer changes the value, which includes a zero interval and floating-point resolution limits) it sets at to ev_rt_now and stops; otherwise it sets at = nat and repeats. It then stores at in ev_at(w). The result is therefore a time greater than ev_rt_now when the loop advanced it, the initial value if that already exceeded ev_rt_now, or exactly ev_rt_now in the stalled-addition case. With a negative w->interval the loop moves at backwards and ends only when the addition stops changing at; no other memory is modified.
note: ev.c:3366-3388 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (a negative interval does not advance at, so the loop does not end by passing ev_rt_now); reviewer 2 right (a zero interval ends the loop at once with at = ev_rt_now, 3378-3381); reviewer 3 right (a negative interval can end through the nat == at test).

name: CLeashApp::ProbeKDC
prose: Windows Leash method (Leash.cpp:982-1065) that checks whether a KDC answers by trying a login for a throw-away user; it returns a BOOL (TRUE or FALSE) and takes no arguments. If the function pointer pkrb5_init_context is NULL it returns FALSE at once. Otherwise it zeroes a creds structure and tries, in order, pkrb5_init_context, pkrb5_cc_default and pkrb5_cc_get_principal; if getting the principal from the default cache fails it falls back to parsing the principal "foo" with pkrb5_parse_name, and only if that also fails does it go to cleanup. Any failure of these steps (or of pkrb5_build_principal, which builds the probe principal PROBE_USERNAME in the realm of that principal) goes to cleanup and the function returns FALSE. It fills a 16-byte password with pkrb5_c_random_make_octets; if that fails it runs a refill loop whose counter is never incremented (the for statement has no increment, line 1026), so the function does not return in that case. It NUL-terminates the password and calls pkrb5_get_init_creds_password with the probe principal, no prompter, no options. The result TRUE is returned exactly when that call returns KRB5KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, KRB5KDC_ERR_CLIENT_REVOKED, KRB5KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NOTYET, KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED or KRB5KDC_ERR_PADATA_TYPE_NOSUPP (a KDC answered); success or any other error gives FALSE. After the early NULL-pointer return, every path reaches cleanup, which clears creds.client when it equals probeprinc, frees the credentials contents, frees the principals and closes the ccache and frees the context where they are non-NULL, and returns the result.
note: Leash.cpp:980-1065 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewers right: a pkrb5_cc_get_principal failure does not by itself return 0 because the fallback pkrb5_parse_name("foo") may succeed and continue (1008-1012).

name: CLeashView::OnTrayIcon
prose: Windows Leash handler (LeashView.cpp:1743-1810) for tray-icon notifications; lParam carries the mouse message and wParam is not used. For WM_LBUTTONDOWN it calls OnLeashRestore when CMainFrame::m_isMinimum is set and OnLeashMinimize otherwise. For WM_RBUTTONDOWN it allocates a CMenu, creates a popup menu and appends a "Close/Open MIT Kerberos Window" item (depending on m_isMinimum), a separator and "Get Tickets"; it then waits INFINITE on ticketinfo.lockObj and throws "Unable to lock ticketinfo" if the wait does not return WAIT_OBJECT_0 (for WAIT_ABANDONED the thread has been given the mutex and the throw leaves it held; in every throwing case the already created menu is not destroyed or deleted). With the mutex held it appends "Renew Tickets", grayed unless ticketinfo.Krb5.btickets is non-zero and CLeashApp::m_hKrb5DLL is set, computes a gray flag for the Destroy item from btickets but then releases the mutex and appends "Destroy Tickets" with plain MF_STRING (the computed flag is not used, so that item is never grayed here), appends "Change Password", a separator, "Automatic Ticket Renewal" and "Expiration Alarm" (checked according to m_autoRenewTickets and m_lowTicketAlarm), a separator and "Exit". It sets ID_LEASH_RESTORE as the default item, gets the cursor position, calls SetForegroundWindow, tracks the popup at the cursor (TPM_RIGHTALIGN | TPM_RIGHTBUTTON, owner the parent frame), posts WM_NULL, destroys the menu and deletes the CMenu. WM_MOUSEMOVE and any other lParam do nothing. It returns 0 on every path that does not throw.
note: LeashView.cpp:1743-1810 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (the old contract hid the throw path); reviewer 2 right (WAIT_ABANDONED grants ownership and the function leaves it held when it throws, 1763-1764); reviewer 3 right (Destroy Tickets is appended with MF_STRING only, 1776, the computed gray flag at 1771-1774 is never used).

name: CLeashView::OnObtainTGTWithParam
prose: Windows Leash message handler (LeashView.cpp:2277-2323) that shows the "get ticket" dialog, optionally preset from a shared-memory block; wParam is unused and lParam is either 0 or a file-mapping handle. It fills an LSH_DLGINFO_EX with the size, DLGTYPE_PASSWD, use_defaults 1 and pointers to its in.title, in.username and in.realm buffers (the structure is not zeroed first, so those buffers keep whatever bytes they had unless set below). If lParam is non-zero it maps the object with MapViewOfFile (read/write, 4096 bytes). If the mapping succeeded it reads up to four consecutive NUL-terminated strings from it, in the order title, username, realm and ccache, copying each non-empty one with strcpy_s into the dialog structure; the pointer is advanced past each string with strlen, with no check that the strings fit inside the 4096 mapped bytes. If lParam is 0 or the mapping failed it sets only the title to "MIT Kerberos: Get Ticket". If the username and realm strings are both non-empty it ORs DLGFLAG_READONLYPRINC into ldi.dlgtype. It calls pLeash_kinit_dlg_ex(m_hWnd, &ldi) and keeps its result. It then calls UnmapViewOfFile on the param pointer, which has been advanced past the strings by then, so the view that MapViewOfFile returned is not the address that is passed (the mapping is not properly unmapped on the success path), closes the lParam handle if it was non-zero, sends WM_COMMAND with ID_UPDATE_DISPLAY to its own window and returns the dialog result.
note: LeashView.cpp:2277-2323 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer right: UnmapViewOfFile receives the advanced pointer (2300-2318), so the mapped view is not unmapped through its base address when strings were read.

name: main
prose: Test-file runner of libecc's arithmetic tests (arithmetic_tests.c:883-1233; the packet called it an unnamed excerpt, the function is main). It initialises seven nn values and the generic fp/nn parameter pools (failure: error path, which returns -1). With WITH_ASSERT_BACKTRACE it installs a SIGINT handler (failure returns -1). With more than 2 arguments it returns -1; with the single argument "-info" it prints WORDSIZE and NN_MAX_BASE and returns 0. It mallocs the input buffer (NULL: return -1), opens the file named by argv[1] with open (the result is not checked) or uses standard input, and reads lines with read_string. For each line it parses the test number (asserted equal to the line counter), the operation name and the parameter type string, returning -1 directly if one of those three separators is missing. It then parses each record by its type letter: 'c' (a field context: a second 'c' in the same line, or a mismatch between the imported and the computed r, r_square, mpinv, p_shift or p_reciprocal, goes to err; a mismatch of the normalised p returns -1 directly), 'f' (needs a prior context, a limit of pre-allocated fp values), 'p' (a raw pointer record whose value must be 0, else err), 'n' (more than the pre-allocated number returns -1 directly), 'u' and 's' (decimal numbers), and any other letter goes to err. It records the type string, finds the test function for the operation in the dispatch table (an unknown operation is skipped with a message), calls it, adds 1 to oktests when it returns 1, and resets the counters for the next line. After the last line it prints the number of OK tests, total tests and NOK tests, closes the file if its descriptor is non-zero, frees the buffer and returns 0, so a run with failing tests still returns 0. The err label prints a message, closes the file if non-zero, frees the buffer and returns -1; the direct -1 returns above do not close the file or free the buffer.
note: arithmetic_tests.c:883-1233 read (the printf lines skipped). Reviewer right in substance: the old prose already listed the direct -1 returns; corrected here that the function returns 0 even when tests failed, and that the open result is not checked.

name: GENERIC_TEST(test_name, operation_, given_string_helper, fun_name, parameters_types_, parameters_io_, parameters_string_names, fun_output, nn_out_num, fp_out_num, ...)
prose: Macro (arithmetic_tests.c:496-627) that generates a test function int test_<test_name>(const char *op, void **params, int test_num) and registers it in the dispatch table with ADD_TO_DISPATCH_TABLE; the packet slice ended before the tail of the body. Generated function: it asserts that op equals the operation name string; returns -1 (after a message) if the global parameter-type string global_parameters differs from the declared parameter types; runs PARAMETERS_SANITY_CHECK, which returns 0 after a message when a type is not one of c, f, n, u, s, when an I/O letter is not i, o or O, when an 'O' parameter is not of type u or s, or when more than one 'O' output is declared. It then takes the common word length n_len from the first output parameter of type 'f' or 'n' and the field context from the first 'c' parameter, declares and initialises the nn and fp output temporaries with the GENERIC_TEST_NN/FP_DECL_INIT macros (a non-zero ret goes to err, which prints a message and calls exit(-1)), asserts that fp outputs are only used when a context exists, and calls the tested function with the given arguments through CHECK_FUN_<fun_output>. It then looks up the operation's printable name and, for each parameter marked 'o', compares the computed value with the expected input value (fp_cmp for 'f', nn_cmp for 'n', direct comparison for 'u' and 's') and compares the function's return value with the 'O' parameter; at the first mismatch or failed comparison it prints "result mismatch", dumps all values with PRINT_ALL and sets mismatch. It then uninitialises the temporaries and returns !mismatch (1 when every compared value matched, 0 otherwise).
note: arithmetic_tests.c:346-372 and 496-627 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewers: only the mechanical name rejection was recorded; the earlier prose was written from a slice that ended before the comparison part, which is now covered. Named as the macro definition head per the method.

name: GENERIC_TEST(test_name, operation_, given_string_helper, fun_name, parameters_types_, parameters_io_, parameters_string_names, fun_output, nn_out_num, fp_out_num, ...)
prose: Macro (arithmetic_tests.c:496-627; GENERIC_TEST_NN and GENERIC_TEST_FP at 629-633 wrap it) that generates int test_<test_name>(const char *op, void **params, int test_num) and registers it in the dispatch table. In the generated function: assert(memcmp(operation, op, ...) == 0); return -1 after a message if global_parameters differs from the declared parameter types; PARAMETERS_SANITY_CHECK may return 0 (bad type letter, bad I/O letter, an 'O' parameter of a type other than u or s, or more than one 'O'); it derives n_len and the field context from the parameters, initialises the nn/fp temporaries (initialisation failure prints an error and calls exit(-1)), calls the function under test, and compares each 'o' parameter (fp_cmp, nn_cmp, or direct word/int comparison) and the 'O' return value against the expected values from the test file; at the first mismatch it prints "result mismatch" and a dump of the inputs, real and expected values and stops comparing. It clears the temporaries and returns 1 when everything matched and 0 on a mismatch.
note: arithmetic_tests.c:496-627 read in full. Reviewers: only the mechanical name rejection and unreviewed state were recorded.
